claim: Anchoring on numeric estimates is a large, replicable group-level effect in humans (Many Labs 1: all four items replicated; Schley 2026: +0.57 item SD, N=1,967; cross-culture r 0.26 to 0.61).
agent_test: Give the same estimate question with no hint, low hint, high hint; measure shift in SD units at equal tokens.
audit_note: Minor: 'cross-culture r 0.26 to 0.61' are pooled meta-analytic correlations for four items with high heterogeneity (I2 65-87%); 'all four Many Labs 1 items replicated' follows from Kakinohana et al. (anchoring a successful Many Labs 1 replication; all four meta-analytic effects p<.001) rather than a direct read of Klein 2014.

claim: In Many Labs 2 the incidental-anchor effect of Critcher and Gilovich 2008 (phone name P97 vs P17) did not replicate (d=0.04, 95% CI [-0.01, 0.09], N=6,826 vs original d=0.30, N=207); Wikipedia reports random-anchor studies (die roll, random button) also failed to replicate, and in Schley and Weingarten's explicit-anchor study (N=1,967) the effect was larger when the anchor applied to the target judgment and was farther from the centre of unanchored beliefs.
agent_test: Compare relevant vs clearly irrelevant numbers in the prompt; check whether the agent ignores irrelevant ones.
audit_note: Numbers verify (Many Labs 2: d=0.30 N=207 vs d=0.04 [-0.01,0.09] N=6,826), but they come from one incidental-anchor paradigm (Critcher and Gilovich 2008 phone-name study), so 'incidental anchors do not replicate' is wider than the evidence; Schley and Weingarten support relevance and distance as moderators for explicit anchors only.
claim_before_audit: Incidental (task-irrelevant) anchors do not replicate in humans: Many Labs 2 d=0.04 (N=6,826) vs original d=0.30 (N=207). Relevance to the target and distance from belief drive the effect.

claim: Many Labs 2 replicated 15 of 28 findings (54 percent) with median d falling from 0.60 to 0.15; classic H&B effects that survive shrink in size, so lab effect sizes are upper bounds.
agent_test: Do not set bias-correction strength from original lab sizes; calibrate on the agent itself.

claim: Risky-choice (gain/loss) framing persists: DeKay (2025, N=1,697) found a framing effect for completely described, matched options (OR=1.84, 95% CI for b [0.29, 0.93]) and in seven of nine matched comparisons, while part of the classic effect depends on mismatched option wording. Separately, Many Labs 2 replicated the Tversky and Kahneman 1981 Study 10 cheap/costly-item framing at roughly half the original size (OR 4.96 to 2.06; d 1.08 to 0.40), which is a different framing task, not a risky-choice problem.
agent_test: Write each option fully and symmetrically; test whether the agent's choice flips with gain vs loss wording.
audit_note: Numbers verify (ML2 jacket/calculator OR 4.96 to 2.06, d 1.08 to 0.40; DeKay OR 1.84), but the ML2 item is Tversky and Kahneman 1981 Study 10 (cheap vs costly item, mental accounting), not a gain/loss risky-choice problem, so it is not evidence about risky-choice framing weakening; the claim's own caveat contradicts using it as the headline.
claim_before_audit: Gain/loss risky-choice framing replicates in humans but weaker than the original (jacket/calculator item OR 4.96 to 2.06; DeKay 2025 OR 1.84 for matched complete options); part of the effect is mismatched option wording. Primary re-read (d14): the Many Labs 2 framing item is T&K 1981 Study 10 (d 1.08 to 0.40), not the Asian disease problem; the Asian disease numbers (72/78 percent) are still second-hand.

claim: The Linda conjunction error depends on wording and format: about 85 percent original, 57 percent with 'whether or not', about 20 percent with frequency format; the frequency-format account is contested. Review in d15: Fiedler 1988 found a frequency gain, Wedell and Moro 2007 found none; natural-frequency advantage was not found for joint probabilities (Stegmueller 2024).
agent_test: Ask Linda-type items in probability vs natural-frequency format and compare error.

claim: Base-rate neglect is task-dependent: with no sketch people use the base rate, with a worthless sketch they say .5; small-sample insensitivity is common (hospital: 53 of 95 'about the same').
agent_test: Force a base-rate line (reference class) before reading case details; measure Bayes error on cab-type items.
audit_note: Numbers verified in Tversky and Kahneman 1974 (no description: base rates used; worthless description: .5; hospital 21/21/53 = 95 students), but both listed primary entries are the same 1974 paper and Wikipedia just relays it; 'small-sample insensitivity is common' rests on one student question.

claim: Availability judgments depend on ease of retrieval, not only the number of examples recalled: in Schwarz and colleagues' study (as reported on Wikipedia, primary not read) participants who recalled 12 assertive behaviours, a hard task, rated themselves less assertive than those who recalled 6; Vaughn (1999), as reported there, found the effect of listed-example count only when uncertainty was high (start of semester, hardest exam); Tversky and Kahneman (1974) showed availability-type biases in committee-count estimates (median 70 for 2-member vs 20 for 8-member committees; correct answer 45).
agent_test: Ask the agent to list 6 vs 12 examples before a frequency judgement; look for ease-of-retrieval flip.
audit_note: T&K 1974 supports the committee-estimate availability bias, but the ease-of-retrieval and moderator findings (Schwarz 1991, Vaughn 1999) were only read second-hand via Wikipedia, and the Schwarz result is that recalling 12 assertive examples gave lower assertiveness self-ratings than recalling 6 (and the reverse for unassertive recall), not that 12 examples generally lower self-ratings.
claim_before_audit: Availability depends on ease of retrieval, not only count, and moderators (uncertainty, relevance) matter; recalling 12 examples gives lower self-ratings than 6.

claim: Incentives reduce the conjunction fallacy only slightly (meta-analysis d=0.19, N=3,276, preprint, not opened); cognitive ability and reflection predict fewer errors.
agent_test: Token budget plays the role of incentive: test whether more tokens cut errors on conjunction items.

claim: Anchoring has poor reliability as an individual-difference measure (split-half lowest of the tasks), so single-item agent runs are noisy.
agent_test: Use many items and repeats per condition; report variance, not one run.

claim: LLMs show human-like anchoring: ChatGPT low 20.83 vs high 105.97 (humans 22.50 vs 80.50); GPT-4 22.0 vs 94.33 (5 trials); GPT-3.5/4/4o anchored on 62 questions.
agent_test: Same anchor protocol on our agent with and without scaffold at equal tokens.
audit_note: Minor: GPT-4 figures come from only 5 trials per cell.

claim: Anchoring in LLMs is wide: 22 to 61 percent of questions anchored across 11 models, mean bias score 0.39 across 20 models; reasoning models are least anchored. But Kraishan 2026 (7 models, matched siblings) found no reliable reasoning advantage (+0.031, p=.157) and Yao 2026 found thinking raised adoption of an authority-tagged anchor in 6 of 7 models; "reasoning models are least anchored" rests on one benchmark (Huang).
agent_test: Measure anchored share per question for the base model and the scaffolded agent.

claim: Simple prompt fixes do not remove LLM anchoring: CoT, 'ignore the anchor', principles and reflection leave significant anchor effects (Lou and Sun); knowledge enhancement raised Llama-3.1-8B's anchoring ratio from 34.7 to 50.5 percent (Huang); CoT was worse than baseline overall on PROBE-SWE bias sensitivity (16.1 vs 12.9 percent, Sovrano); in code review, a weak ignore-context prompt left combined attack success at 83 to 88 percent on four open models while a stronger one lowered it to 49 to 88 percent (Shahriar); a verbalise-the-anchor line lowered anchoring on 5 of 5 items but only at p=.057 (Kraishan).
agent_test: Run CoT vs ignore-anchor vs generate-own-estimate-first at equal tokens.
audit_note: Lou and Sun, Huang (Llama-3.1-8B 34.7 to 50.5), Sovrano (CoT 16.1 vs 12.9 baseline) and Kraishan (p=.057) check out, but in Shahriar et al. the 83-88% combined attack success is the weak defense; the strong ignore-context defense cut it to 88.45 (LLaMA 4), 69.23 (LLaMA 3), 49.32 (DeepSeek) and 67.80 (Qwen).
claim_before_audit: Simple prompt fixes do not remove LLM anchoring: CoT, 'ignore the anchor', principles, reflection fail (Lou & Sun); knowledge enhancement raised it 34.7 to 50.5 percent (Huang); CoT gave no per-bias gain in SE tasks (Sovrano). Also: telling code-review models to ignore metadata left combined attack success at 83 to 88 percent on four open models (d06); a restate-every-number line lowered anchoring on 5 of 5 items but at p=.057 (d04).

claim: Showing both a low and a high anchor removes the pull on questions where hints straddle the benchmark, not on others.
agent_test: Counter-anchor prompt: supply opposing anchors; test on straddling vs non-straddling items.

claim: Self-debiasing by rewriting the prompt works better than few-shot: leftover biased prompt elements 0 to 2.7 percent for framing in GPT-4/Llama; iterative detect-analyse-rewrite (SACD) cuts FOMC bias score from 0.38 to 0.16 for llama3.1-8b.
agent_test: Prompt-rewriting step at S1 vs none, equal total tokens, measure bias score.

claim: Few-shot examples, Reflexion and multi-agent debate can raise bias by feeding biased text back (debate 0.50 vs vanilla 0.38 on FOMC).
agent_test: Check that critique steps do not copy the biased frame; ablate debate.
audit_note: Debate 0.502 vs vanilla 0.3805 is llama3.1-8b FOMC average; Reflexion average (0.383) is about equal to vanilla and few-shot rise is smaller; Lyu itself calls few-shot inconsistent. Substance holds.

claim: Eliciting domain best practices first and injecting them cut bias sensitivity by about 51 percent on average (up to 73 percent) on 8 biases in software-engineering dilemmas; anchoring sensitivity is low at baseline (5.9 percent).
agent_test: Best-practices-first step before the task, equal tokens.

claim: LLM framing effect is strong: GPT-4 admits 40.5 percent more under reject framing; GPT-3 mirrors the Asian disease reversal (die frame 74 percent risky) with a boundary at high save probability; framing mean bias 0.41 across 20 models. Caveat: on 5 Malberg framing items, seven 2025 models leaned against the human direction (mean -0.336), so framing effects in current models depend on item and scoring.
agent_test: Run paired gain/loss rewrites of the same decision; require invariance.
audit_note: The Jones & Steinhardt 2022 paper (arXiv 2202.12299) is about Codex and GPT-3 anchoring/framing of code and estimates and contains no Asian disease experiment, 704 prompts, 74% die-frame figure or save-probability boundary; the other numbers (GPT-4 40.5%, Malberg framing 0.41, Kraishan -0.336 on five items, seven models) check out.

claim: Code models copy irrelevant earlier prompt content: accuracy 32.9 to 2.4 percent (Codex) with an irrelevant function plus framing line, framing line output 91.7 percent for one line (81 percent averaged over five lines).
agent_test: Insert irrelevant material in the context; measure accuracy drop with and without a relevance filter.

claim: Instruction tuning and RLHF increase decoy, certainty and belief biases relative to base models.
agent_test: Compare base-like and tuned decoding on decoy items if both are available.

claim: LLM errors on H&B tasks are mostly not the human bias: GPT-4 69.2 percent correct with correct reasoning, only 21.7 percent of GPT-3.5 answers human-like biased; answers vary across repeats.
agent_test: Repeat each item 10 times; score consistency as well as correctness.

claim: Item rewrites break LLM performance: GPT-3 correct or human-like on 12 of 12 standard vignettes, non-human errors on adversarial rewrites; new Linda/Bill vignettes put models near chance (0.46 to 0.53) vs humans 0.56 to 0.83; option-order effects large in models.
agent_test: Use fresh paraphrased vignettes and shuffle option order; contamination control.

claim: Older GPT-3 models fall for CRT traps more than humans (80 percent intuitive vs 55); ChatGPT-3.5 and GPT-4 mostly do not (59 and 96 percent correct vs 38). CoT lifts davinci-003 from 5 to 28 percent correct.
agent_test: CRT-type items with and without forced reasoning at equal tokens.

claim: Anchoring is not universal in LLMs: GPT-3 showed essentially no anchoring in a code-completion length task (means 41.5 vs 41.28), though two experiments gave small significant gaps (3 to 4 points).
agent_test: Check anchoring with several task framings; do not assume one task type.

claim: LLM judges show order, bandwagon (over 70 percent follow the cue) and self-preference bias; about 40 percent of comparisons biased. Order swap changed verdicts in 5 to 82.5 percent of comparisons (GPT-4 and ChatGPT, Wang 2023); position consistency 23.8 to 65.0 percent across Claude-v1, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 (Zheng 2023); robustness below 0.5 with 3 to 4 candidates (Ye 2024).
agent_test: Randomise candidate order; for close calls only, swap and require agreement (2x tokens); use a different model from the generator.
audit_note: Ye: only most (not all) judge models fell below 0.5 robustness at 3-4 candidates.

claim: Anchoring acts in early layers and pre-answer anchors resist prompt or decoding changes (Anti-DP 24.7 vs 34.7 percent baseline is the only mild gain).
agent_test: Prefer input-side removal (S1 rewrite) over output-side fixes.

claim: There is no formal computational model of the three heuristics; they remain verbal, with partial models for anchoring only.
agent_test: None; treat the heuristics as a checklist of tests, not a model.

claim: More thinking tokens do not reliably reduce bias in current reasoning models: pooled reasoning-minus-sibling bias +0.031 (p=.157), no negative dose-response slope for any of four model families over realised 0 to 2,800 tokens, 12,350 calls.
agent_test: Run the same 30 judgment items with thinking off and on for the agent model, 10 repeats each, and compare signed scores.

claim: Thinking can strengthen adoption of an anchor that looks credible: 6 of 7 models amplified an authority-tagged anchor under thinking, and 3 flipped sign by source credibility (abstract only).
agent_test: Strip the source label from any number before the thinking step; compare adoption of low- vs high-credibility attributions.

claim: Among six biases tested in seven 2025 models, only numeric anchoring pointed in the human direction (mean +0.163, d=1.89); framing, loss aversion, escalation and confirmation leaned against it and availability was absent.
agent_test: Prioritise numeric-anchor tests; treat the other biases as item-dependent checks.

claim: Context-borne framing, anchoring and halo cues flip vulnerability verdicts in all eight LLMs tested (framing 33.2, anchoring 23.5, halo 18.4 percent mean susceptibility), and prompt-level defences do not fix it.
agent_test: Filter non-code context (descriptions, author, prior verdicts) from the checker input and compare with the unfiltered run.

claim: In long-horizon agents, early interpretations persist and stored model-written insights mislead: removing insight memory raised Hit@5 from 0.526 to 0.601 (Qwen3-235B); self-referential multi-turn context shifts confidence differently per model (Claude -0.032, p=.029; N=15).
agent_test: Compare an agent reading its own stored conclusions against one reading only raw evidence on a drifting task.

claim: Cloned agents add up a shared anchor rather than cancelling it: a one-sentence anchor to sellers cut market efficiency from 96 to 15 percent; a one-line debiasing instruction reversed it (abstract only).
agent_test: Critique steps should use a differently framed input, not a copy of the proposer prompt.

claim: Human anchoring moderators: expertise lowers and anchor extremity raises anchoring, relevance had no effect (two preregistered experiments, abstract only). In LLMs, stronger models are anchored more consistently and time-period answers resist anchoring (6 of 11 exceptions from 17 percent of questions).
agent_test: Sweep anchor extremity and prior-knowledge cues on the agent model.

claim: Scoring choice changes whether anchoring is detected: a categorical within-50%-of-anchor rule found no predictor effect where aggregate directional gaps show anchoring (human, abstract only).
agent_test: Pre-register the scoring rule (directional low-vs-high gap) before agent tests.
